title: The Founder Bottleneck
sub: A week of LinkedIn posts about what stops when everything has to go through the founder.
description: A LinkedIn campaign for B2Ne in three chapters: what it costs when every deal, decision and customer call waits for the founder. Concept, copy, design, video and posting by Riya Dutta.
facts: Founders of small and mid-sized B2B tech companies
Everything, end to end: concept, copy, design, video, posting and reading the results. I run B2Ne’s LinkedIn campaigns on my own.

hero.alt: The Sick Day post: You stayed home. So did the pipeline.

sections.title: The founder is the bottleneck.
sections.lead: Every proposal, renewal and customer call waits for one person, so the company only moves as fast as their calendar.
sections.close: Each post shows one ordinary moment where that happens, and ends on the question a founder would rather not answer.

sections.title: One week, three chapters.
sections.intro: Each chapter names a different cost, so the week builds from the founder’s evenings to their buyers to next year.

items.d: The work that waits for you after hours: the open proposal, the holiday laptop, the sick day, the sleepless night.
A demo slot three weeks out, customers who only call you, a new customer explaining everything twice.
The new hire who has to “check with the founder”, and growth that adds jobs instead of handing them away.

sections.title: Fifteen pieces, in posting order.
sections.intro: Pick a stamp to see the post, play the video or swipe the carousel, and read the caption that went out with it.

items.title: The Night Shift
items.text:
Your team logged off hours ago.
But the proposal, the pricing question and the follow-up only you can send are still open on your laptop.
So dinner waits. Then the evening goes.
The work didn't stop. It waited for you.
What's still waiting on you tonight?

items.title: The Holiday Laptop
items.text:
You set the out-of-office, then packed the laptop anyway.
Because the renewal call, last week's demo follow-up and a new inbound lead can't move without you.
So you check email by the pool and reply before breakfast.
You took the holiday. Not the break.
When did you last switch off for a full week?

items.title: The Sick Day
items.text:
You were ill for one day. Nothing dramatic.
But no demo got booked, no renewal got signed, and every call moved to next week.
Not because the team didn't care. Because none of it could move without you.
Your pipeline has one heartbeat.
What stops when you're out for a day?

items.title: The Sleepless Night
items.text:
Last night: lights off, then your mind started.
The renewal that's due on Friday. The demo you still need to prepare. The lead you haven't replied to.
None of it is written down anywhere else, and nobody else is following it.
So you carried it to bed.
Which deal kept you up last night?

items.title: The Only Copy
items.text:
Ask how deals get closed here, and the answer is a person.
The pricing logic, the objections buyers always raise, why the last buyer actually said yes. It's all real. It just lives in your head, your notebook and your inbox.
So every new hire starts from zero, and every deal comes back to you.
Your sales process has one copy.
Where does yours live?

items.title: The Gym Bag
items.text:
The gym bag's been packed since Monday.
But every evening, a customer call, a proposal or a question only you can answer turns up at five.
So the bag goes back in the hallway, unopened.
The deal got your evening. Again.
What's the first thing you drop when the week gets busy?

items.title: The Long Wait
items.text:
Your buyer asked a simple question on Monday: can you send us a quote?
But only you could answer, and you were in back-to-back calls until Wednesday.
By then, someone else had replied within the hour.
The buyer didn't choose the better product. They chose the answer.
Who answers your buyers when you can't?

items.title: The Demo Slot
items.text:
Next free demo slot: three weeks from now.
Only you can give the demo, and your calendar is already full.
So the buyer who asked on Wednesday books a demo with someone else for tomorrow.
Three weeks is a long time to stay interested.
How far out is your next free demo slot?

items.title: Every Customer Calls You
items.text:
"Can I speak to the founder?"
Early on, that's a compliment. Buyers trust you, so every call, every question and every renewal comes to you.
But trust that lives in one person can't be in two calls at once.
So the more buyers trust you, the slower everything moves.
Trust with one name doesn't scale.
Which of your customers would happily talk to someone else on your team?

items.title: Explains Everything Twice
items.text:
Your new customer explained everything on the sales call. Their setup, their deadline, the one thing that must not break.
But it stayed in your head and your notes. So when your team took over, they asked for all of it again.
The customer's first week with you was a repeat of the sale.
What does your team know about a new customer on day one?

items.title: Contact Us
items.text:
Your buyer read your website at eleven at night, before ever talking to you.
But every real answer was behind "contact us", because the answers only live in your head.
So they found a site that explained itself, and booked a call there instead.
What can a buyer learn from your website without talking to you?

items.title: Signed, Then Silence
items.text:
Your best customer hasn't heard from you in months.
Not because you don't care. Every call to them still waits for you.
And you've been busy closing the next one.
They noticed.

items.title: The Bottleneck
items.text:
Next year's plan says more deals. You've already told the team.
But this week, quotes still sat waiting for your reply.
So next year's extra deals won't turn into extra revenue. The extra ones will spill.

items.title: Let Me Check
items.text:
Next year you hire a salesperson. In week one, a customer asks for a discount.
They answer: "Let me check with the founder."
But you're in another meeting. And the next customer gets the same answer.
So you didn't hire a salesperson. You hired a messenger.

items.title: Every Job
items.text:
Someone asks what you do. You say founder. Then you keep going.
The company you started to build bigger than you now runs on your job list.
And next year's growth won't hand those jobs away. It adds new ones.

sections.title: Lamp light against laptop light.
sections.note: Night scenes throughout: warm amber lamp light against the cold blue of a laptop, so the cost always lands after hours.
